Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette:
Renata Kowalski is a 54-year-old married woman of Polish descent who has worked as a chef for nearly three decades, most recently as the head chef at a mid-sized restaurant in the city where she has lived with her husband for the past twenty years. She came to the initial intake session composed but visibly guarded, choosing a seat with her back to the wall and tracking the door throughout the conversation. She described herself as someone who had always prided herself on her competence and self-sufficiency, qualities she believed had served her well across a demanding career. What brought her to treatment, she said quietly, was the recognition that she could no longer manage on her own.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Renata was assaulted by a male colleague - a sous-chef she had worked alongside for six years, a man she had mentored, advocated for, and trusted without reservation. The assault occurred late on a weeknight after the kitchen had closed, when the two of them were alone finishing inventory. He had moved toward her suddenly, and what followed happened in a space she now cannot fully reconstruct in language. She has tried many times to write it down or explain it clearly, even to herself, and finds that the experience resists being put into words - not because she chooses silence, but because the event seems to exist in a register that precedes language. What she does have are pieces: the sound of a walk-in refrigerator door, the particular angle at which she was pressed against a steel counter, a smell she cannot name but that returns without warning. These fragments arrive without sequence and without the sense that they belong to a coherent story she can hold at a distance. When they surface, she does not merely remember - her shoulders curl forward, her arms draw inward, her body returning to the posture of that night as though the interval between then and now had briefly ceased to exist.

In the weeks after the assault, Renata continued going to work because she could not imagine what stopping would mean. But the kitchen, which had always been her domain, became a landscape of threat. Unexpected movement - a line cook stepping quickly into her peripheral vision, a server pushing through the swing door - would produce an immediate physical response, her body bracing before her mind had registered anything. She became hypervigilant in a way that exhausted her, scanning the room constantly, noting where every person stood, who was approaching and from which direction. Strangers entering the kitchen for deliveries felt dangerous in a way she could not justify to herself but could not override. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like knowledge rather than fear, that there was simply no way to know which man would harm her - that the six years she had spent trusting her colleague had demonstrated only her own blindness. The betrayal felt less like an event than a revelation about the nature of people, and she found herself measuring everyone against it.

Over the following months, Renata began finding reasons to ensure she was never alone in a room with a male colleague. She rearranged scheduling in ways that her staff noticed. She shortened conversations that moved toward anything personal or emotionally weighted, deflecting with efficiency and humor until the other person withdrew. Her husband, a patient man who had initially responded to her withdrawal with gentle concern, had grown quieter himself. She was aware that she had placed a distance between them she did not fully understand how to close, and that his attempts at emotional closeness now produced in her something close to panic, though she had not told him this. Their evenings, once companionable, had become careful.

What finally brought Renata to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when a trusted female colleague placed a hand on her arm during a difficult conversation, and Renata felt herself go entirely cold. She drove home and sat in her car for an hour. She had not cried. What she felt instead was a clear and frightening recognition that she was disappearing from her own life. She came to treatment hoping, she said, to understand what had happened to her. What she feared most was that the answer would confirm what she had already begun to suspect - that the person she had been before that night was simply gone.
